questions.q: What role does this lesson say raw activation visualization typically plays in an interpretability workflow?
options: It is the final, conclusive step that replaces all other methods once completed
It requires retraining the model from scratch each time
It can only be used after a probing classifier has already been trained
It is usually a first exploratory step that surfaces candidate patterns worth investigating further with more rigorous methods
questions.explain: The lesson frames visualization as exploratory: look first, hypothesize, then verify with more rigorous methods, rather than as a replacement for deeper analysis.

questions.q: What visual signature does the lesson describe as characteristic of a previous-token head?
options: A bright band one step below the main diagonal in the attention heatmap, showing each position attending to the position just before it
A completely blank attention matrix with all zero values
An attention pattern that only ever attends to the first token in the sequence
A uniform attention weight spread evenly across all positions
questions.explain: A sub-diagonal bright band means each query position consistently attends to the key one step earlier — the classic visual signature of a previous-token head, a building block of induction heads.

questions.q: In the neuron activation trace example, what does plotting a single neuron's activation across token positions help reveal?
options: The total number of parameters in the model
The learning rate used during training
The exact training loss curve of the model
A candidate neuron that spikes reliably on a specific token type or category, worth investigating further
questions.explain: A neuron trace that spikes on a particular token type or syntactic boundary is a candidate for closer study, the kind of observation that motivates more rigorous feature-decomposition work.

questions.q: Why does this lesson caution against over-interpreting a single neuron's visualized activation pattern?
options: Because neurons never produce any observable activation values
Because activation values are always identical across all neurons
Because of superposition: a single neuron in a realistic model often encodes a mixture of multiple, often unrelated features, not one clean concept
Because PyTorch hooks are unreliable and often return incorrect values
questions.explain: Superposition means a neuron's activation trace can look suggestively specific without corresponding to one tidy, isolated human concept.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a vivid attention pattern is not, on its own, a rigorous causal explanation of the model's output?
options: Because attention weights show where weight is directed, which is suggestive but a separate claim from a rigorous causal account of why the final output was produced
Because attention patterns are identical across every layer of every model
Because attention patterns are randomly generated and carry no information
Because attention visualization can only be performed on untrained models
questions.explain: Seeing where attention weight goes is a useful clue, but establishing that this pattern actually causally drives the output requires further work, such as the attribution methods covered in the next lesson.
